CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the purpose and structure of Use Case Scenarios in software requirements gathering.
Identify stakeholders, users, and their goals within a software project context.
Apply task analysis techniques to decompose user interactions into discrete steps.
Create comprehensive Use Case Scenarios that cover primary, alternative, and edge-case paths.
Analyze interaction contexts to ensure all realistic usage paths are documented.
Evaluate the completeness of a requirements specification against identified use cases.

Topics.Title: Introduction to Use Case Scenarios
Topics.Summary: This topic establishes what Use Case Scenarios are, why they matter, and how they fit into the broader software development process. Students gain a foundational understanding before moving into practice.

Elements.Title: What Is a Use Case Scenario?
Elements.BodyText: A Use Case Scenario is a narrative description of how a user interacts with a system to achieve a specific goal. It captures the sequence of steps, decisions, and outcomes involved in a single interaction path.
Elements.Notes: Use Case Scenarios originated from object-oriented analysis and are widely attributed to Ivar Jacobson. They serve as a bridge between stakeholder needs and technical specifications.

Items.Text: A Use Case Scenario focuses on one goal a user wants to accomplish.
It describes the interaction from the user's perspective, not the system's internal logic.
Scenarios make abstract requirements concrete and testable.
They are written in plain language so both technical and non-technical stakeholders can review them.

Elements.Title: Role of Use Cases in Requirements Gathering
Elements.BodyText: Use cases serve as a primary vehicle for eliciting and documenting software requirements by grounding abstract needs in real user behavior. They ensure that requirements reflect actual usage rather than assumed functionality.
Elements.Notes: Requirements gathered through use cases tend to be more complete and user-centered because they force teams to think about real scenarios rather than system features in isolation.

Items.Text: Use cases translate stakeholder goals into verifiable system behaviors.
They provide a shared reference point for designers, developers, and testers.
Requirements tied to use cases are easier to prioritize and scope.
Use cases reveal gaps in requirements that feature lists alone often miss.

Elements.Title: Key Components of a Use Case
Elements.BodyText: A well-formed use case includes a title, actor, preconditions, main success scenario, alternative flows, and postconditions. Each component ensures the scenario is complete and unambiguous.
Elements.Notes: Some methodologies also include a trigger event and a priority or frequency rating. Keeping components consistent across all use cases in a project improves readability and traceability.

Items.Text: The actor identifies who initiates or participates in the interaction.
Preconditions state what must be true before the scenario begins.
The main success scenario lists the ideal step-by-step flow.
Alternative flows document what happens when the main path is not followed.
Postconditions describe the state of the system after the scenario completes.

Elements.Title: Use Cases vs. User Stories
Elements.BodyText: Use cases and user stories are both tools for capturing requirements, but they differ in scope, format, and level of detail. Understanding the distinction helps teams choose the right tool for their methodology.
Elements.Notes: Agile teams often use user stories for backlog management and use cases for more detailed interaction documentation when complex flows are involved. The two can complement each other.

Items.Text: User stories are brief and focused on value; use cases are detailed and focused on interaction flow.
Use cases explicitly document alternative paths and edge cases, which user stories typically defer.
User stories suit iterative planning; use cases suit thorough upfront specification.
Both methods should keep the user's goal central to the description.

Topics.Title: Identifying Stakeholders and Users
Topics.Summary: Before writing scenarios, students must correctly identify who will interact with the system and who has an interest in its outcomes. This topic covers stakeholder analysis and user classification techniques.

Elements.Title: Defining Stakeholders
Elements.BodyText: Stakeholders are any individuals, groups, or organizations that have an interest in or are affected by the software system. Identifying all stakeholders early prevents overlooked requirements later in the project.
Elements.Notes: Stakeholders are not limited to direct users. They can include business owners, regulatory bodies, maintenance staff, and even third-party systems that interact with the software.

Items.Text: Primary stakeholders directly use or operate the system.
Secondary stakeholders are affected by the system's outputs without directly using it.
Key stakeholders have authority to approve or change requirements.
Failing to identify all stakeholders is a leading cause of requirements gaps.

Elements.Title: Distinguishing Users from Stakeholders
Elements.BodyText: While all users are stakeholders, not all stakeholders are users. Users are the actors who directly interact with the system interface, whereas other stakeholders may only experience its effects.
Elements.Notes: In use case notation, actors represent roles rather than specific individuals. One person may play multiple actor roles, and one role may be filled by many people.

Items.Text: Actors in use cases represent user roles, not named individuals.
A single stakeholder may perform multiple actor roles across different scenarios.
Non-human actors such as external systems or automated processes should also be identified.
Clearly separating users from stakeholders sharpens the focus of each use case.

Elements.Title: Stakeholder Needs vs. User Goals
Elements.BodyText: Stakeholder needs describe the broader business or organizational outcomes desired from the system, while user goals describe what individual users want to accomplish in a specific interaction. Both must be captured and reconciled.
Elements.Notes: Conflicts between stakeholder needs and user goals are common and must be resolved before finalizing requirements. For example, a manager may need detailed audit logs that a user finds intrusive.

Items.Text: Stakeholder needs often drive high-level system objectives and constraints.
User goals drive the specific tasks and workflows the interface must support.
Unresolved conflicts between the two can lead to unusable or non-compliant systems.
Requirements documents should trace each use case back to at least one stakeholder need.

Elements.Title: User Roles and Permissions
Elements.BodyText: Different user roles often require different levels of access and capability within the same system. Mapping roles to use cases ensures the interface and security model reflect real-world responsibilities.
Elements.Notes: Role-based access control (RBAC) decisions are often informed directly by the actor analysis done during use case development. Documenting roles thoroughly at this stage saves significant rework later.

Items.Text: Each distinct role should have its own set of use cases or variations.
Permissions and access restrictions should be noted in relevant use case preconditions.
Role analysis often reveals the need for administrative or configuration use cases.
User roles should be validated with actual representatives of those roles.

Elements.Title: Techniques for Stakeholder Identification
Elements.BodyText: Several structured techniques help analysts systematically identify all relevant stakeholders and user roles. Using multiple techniques reduces the risk of omitting important participants.
Elements.Notes: Common techniques include stakeholder mapping, onion diagrams, interviews, and reviewing organizational charts. Combining methods is recommended for complex projects.

Items.Text: Stakeholder mapping visualizes relationships between different groups and the system.
Reviewing existing documentation such as org charts and process manuals surfaces hidden stakeholders.
Interviews with domain experts often reveal informal users not captured in formal records.
Iterating stakeholder identification throughout the project accounts for evolving requirements.

Topics.Title: Requirements Gathering Techniques
Topics.Summary: This topic covers the practical methods used to elicit requirements from stakeholders and users, with emphasis on the techniques most relevant to writing use cases. Students learn how to gather specifications systematically.

Elements.Title: Overview of Requirements Elicitation
Elements.BodyText: Requirements elicitation is the process of discovering, extracting, and articulating what a system must do by engaging with stakeholders and users. Choosing the right elicitation technique for each context improves the quality and completeness of requirements.
Elements.Notes: Elicitation is not simply asking people what they want; it involves uncovering tacit knowledge, resolving ambiguities, and surfacing needs that stakeholders may not explicitly articulate.

Items.Text: Effective elicitation combines multiple techniques rather than relying on a single method.
Both explicit stated needs and implicit assumed behaviors must be captured.
Requirements elicitation is iterative and continues throughout the project lifecycle.
Poorly elicited requirements are the most cited source of project failure.

Elements.Title: Interviews and Contextual Inquiry
Elements.BodyText: Interviews allow analysts to engage directly with stakeholders to uncover goals, workflows, pain points, and constraints. Contextual inquiry extends this by observing users in their actual work environment.
Elements.Notes: Contextual inquiry is particularly valuable for identifying undocumented workarounds and informal processes that users have normalized. These often reveal critical use cases that would otherwise be missed.

Items.Text: Structured interviews follow a predetermined set of questions for consistency.
Unstructured interviews allow open-ended exploration of stakeholder perspectives.
Contextual inquiry combines observation with on-the-spot questioning.
Notes and recordings from interviews should be reviewed promptly to capture context.

Elements.Title: Workshops and Focus Groups
Elements.BodyText: Collaborative sessions bring multiple stakeholders together to align on requirements, resolve conflicts, and generate use case ideas collectively. Facilitated workshops are especially effective for complex systems with diverse user groups.
Elements.Notes: Joint Application Development (JAD) sessions are a formal workshop methodology used specifically for requirements gathering. They require skilled facilitation to prevent dominant voices from overshadowing others.

Items.Text: Workshops generate requirements more efficiently than individual interviews for shared processes.
Structured activities such as scenario walkthroughs can focus group discussion.
Divergent stakeholder perspectives surfaced in workshops must be documented and resolved.
Remote workshop tools can replicate in-person collaboration when teams are distributed.

Elements.Title: Surveys and Questionnaires
Elements.BodyText: Surveys allow analysts to gather input from large numbers of stakeholders or users quickly and cost-effectively. They are best suited for validating assumptions or gathering quantitative data about usage patterns.
Elements.Notes: Surveys are weak at uncovering unknown requirements but strong at confirming or prioritizing known ones. They work best when used after initial interviews have shaped the question set.

Items.Text: Closed questions produce structured data suitable for analysis and comparison.
Open questions in surveys can surface unexpected needs but require more effort to analyze.
Survey design must avoid leading questions that bias respondents toward expected answers.
Response rates should be tracked to assess whether the sample represents all user groups.

Elements.Title: Document Analysis and Existing System Review
Elements.BodyText: Reviewing existing documentation, legacy systems, and process manuals provides a baseline of current functionality and workflows. This technique is especially valuable when modernizing or replacing an existing system.
Elements.Notes: Existing systems often encode organizational knowledge that no single stakeholder can fully articulate. However, documented processes may not reflect how the system is actually used in practice.

Items.Text: Current system documentation reveals baseline functionality that must be preserved or improved.
Process manuals and standard operating procedures describe expected user workflows.
Gap analysis between documented and observed behavior surfaces undocumented requirements.
Legacy system constraints discovered during review must be flagged as potential risks.

Topics.Title: Task Analysis
Topics.Summary: Task analysis is the systematic study of how users perform their work, breaking interactions down into steps that inform use case writing. This topic gives students practical methods for decomposing user tasks.

Elements.Title: What Is Task Analysis?
Elements.BodyText: Task analysis is a technique for understanding how users accomplish goals by breaking their work into discrete, observable steps and decisions. It provides the behavioral foundation for writing realistic use case scenarios.
Elements.Notes: Task analysis has roots in cognitive psychology and human factors engineering. In HCI and software requirements contexts it is used to ensure interfaces support real cognitive and procedural workflows.

Items.Text: Task analysis examines both what users do and why they do it.
It reveals the mental models users bring to interactions with a system.
Findings from task analysis directly inform the step sequences in use case main flows.
Task analysis can uncover inefficiencies in current workflows that the new system should address.

Elements.Title: Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA)
Elements.BodyText: Hierarchical Task Analysis decomposes a high-level goal into sub-tasks and further into individual actions, creating a tree structure that maps the full scope of a user's work. HTA is one of the most widely used task analysis methods in requirements engineering.
Elements.Notes: HTA notation includes plans that describe the order and conditions under which sub-tasks are performed. These plans translate directly into the flow logic of use case scenarios.

Items.Text: HTA starts with a top-level goal and recursively breaks it into sub-goals and actions.
Plans in HTA describe sequencing rules such as do in order, do in any order, or do if condition.
HTA diagrams make complex workflows visible and easier to communicate to stakeholders.
Each leaf node in an HTA typically corresponds to a single step in a use case scenario.

Elements.Title: Cognitive Task Analysis
Elements.BodyText: Cognitive Task Analysis (CTA) focuses on the knowledge, decisions, and mental processes involved in performing a task, rather than just the observable actions. It is essential for tasks that require expertise, judgment, or complex problem-solving.
Elements.Notes: CTA methods such as Critical Decision Method (CDM) involve structured interviews with domain experts to surface tacit knowledge. This knowledge often reveals conditional flows and edge cases in use cases.

Items.Text: CTA uncovers the decision points users encounter that are invisible in behavioral observation alone.
It is particularly valuable for expert-intensive domains such as medicine, aviation, or finance.
Findings from CTA often generate alternative and exception flows in use case documentation.
CTA requires more time and expertise to conduct than behavioral task analysis methods.

Elements.Title: Mapping Task Analysis to Use Cases
Elements.BodyText: The outputs of task analysis feed directly into use case writing by providing the step sequences, decision points, and alternative paths that define each scenario. This mapping ensures use cases reflect real user behavior rather than assumed workflows.
Elements.Notes: A practical approach is to use HTA outputs as a checklist when drafting use case main flows, then use CTA findings to populate alternative and exception flows.

Items.Text: Each major task or sub-task identified in analysis can become a distinct use case or flow step.
Decision points in task analysis become branching conditions in alternative flows.
Error states identified in task analysis become exception flows in use cases.
Task analysis findings should be reviewed with users to validate accuracy before use cases are written.

Elements.Title: Validating Task Models with Users
Elements.BodyText: Task models must be verified with actual users to ensure they accurately reflect real work practice rather than idealized or assumed behavior. Validation prevents use cases from being built on incorrect assumptions.
Elements.Notes: Walkthrough sessions where users step through the task model and flag inaccuracies are a cost-effective validation method. Even brief validation sessions can reveal significant modeling errors.

Items.Text: User validation sessions should include representatives of all major actor roles.
Users should be asked to perform or describe tasks while the analyst checks against the model.
Discrepancies between the model and actual behavior must be resolved before writing use cases.
Validated task models serve as a durable artifact that supports future maintenance and redesign.

Topics.Title: Writing Use Case Scenarios
Topics.Summary: This topic provides step-by-step guidance for drafting well-structured Use Case Scenarios, including how to frame the scenario, write clear step sequences, and document the full range of flows. Students practice constructing complete use cases.

Elements.Title: Structuring a Use Case Document
Elements.BodyText: A Use Case document follows a consistent template that ensures every scenario is described with the same level of rigor and detail. Consistent structure makes use cases easier to review, trace, and maintain.
Elements.Notes: Teams should agree on a template before writing begins to avoid inconsistency. Many organizations adapt the Cockburn use case template or the UML use case specification format.

Items.Text: Every use case should have a unique identifier for traceability.
The use case name should be a verb phrase describing the goal, such as Submit Order or Reset Password.
The template should be applied uniformly across all use cases in the project.
Version history and approval status should be tracked in the document header.

Elements.Title: Writing the Main Success Scenario
Elements.BodyText: The main success scenario describes the ideal interaction path where everything goes as expected and the user achieves their goal without errors or exceptions. It is written as a numbered sequence of actor and system actions.
Elements.Notes: Steps should alternate between actor actions and system responses. Avoid implementation details; describe what happens, not how the system achieves it technically.

Items.Text: Each step should describe one discrete action or system response.
Steps should be written in active voice from the actor's or system's perspective.
The sequence should be complete enough that a tester could verify each step.
The final step should confirm that the user's goal has been achieved.

Elements.Title: Documenting Alternative Flows
Elements.BodyText: Alternative flows describe valid variations from the main path that still result in the user achieving their goal or a defined outcome. They capture the realistic diversity of how users interact with a system.
Elements.Notes: Alternative flows are often overlooked in early drafts but are critical for building flexible, user-centered interfaces. Each alternative flow should reference the step in the main scenario where the variation begins.

Items.Text: Alternative flows represent different valid choices a user can make at a given step.
Each alternative flow should indicate where it rejoins or diverges from the main scenario.
Common alternative flows include selecting different options, using shortcuts, or canceling an action.
Alternative flows discovered during task analysis should be incorporated systematically.

Elements.Title: Documenting Exception Flows
Elements.BodyText: Exception flows capture what happens when an error, system failure, or invalid input interrupts the normal interaction. They ensure the system handles failure states gracefully and the interface provides appropriate feedback.
Elements.Notes: Exception flows are the primary mechanism for capturing error-handling requirements. Each exception should specify the trigger condition, the system response, and the recovery path if one exists.

Items.Text: Exception flows are triggered by errors, invalid inputs, or unexpected system states.
Each exception flow must describe how the system notifies the user of the problem.
Recovery paths should be defined wherever the user can correct the issue and continue.
Unrecoverable exceptions must specify how the system preserves data and communicates the failure.

Elements.Title: Specifying Preconditions and Postconditions
Elements.BodyText: Preconditions define the state the system and user must be in before the use case can begin, while postconditions define the guaranteed state after the scenario completes successfully. Together they define the boundary conditions for each scenario.
Elements.Notes: Preconditions are not steps in the scenario; they are assumed to be true when the scenario starts. Postconditions can have multiple outcomes corresponding to the main flow and each alternative flow.

Items.Text: Preconditions must be verifiable states, not vague assumptions.
Postconditions for the main flow should reflect successful goal achievement.
Postconditions for alternative flows may reflect partial completion or different valid outcomes.
Clearly defined pre and postconditions make use cases directly usable as test case inputs.

Elements.Title: Writing Clear and Unambiguous Steps
Elements.BodyText: Each step in a use case must be written precisely enough to be unambiguous to all readers, including developers, testers, and non-technical stakeholders. Ambiguity in step descriptions is a direct source of requirement defects.
Elements.Notes: Common sources of ambiguity include vague verbs such as handles or processes, implicit actor references, and steps that combine multiple actions. Reviewing steps with a colleague from a different discipline is an effective quality check.

Items.Text: Avoid vague verbs; prefer specific actions such as clicks, enters, selects, or displays.
Name the actor explicitly in each step rather than using pronouns.
Each step should represent a single action, not a compound sequence.
Technical jargon should be avoided unless the term has been defined in a glossary.

Topics.Title: Enumerating Usage Paths and Edge Cases
Topics.Summary: Comprehensive use case sets must cover not only common workflows but also infrequent, boundary, and edge case scenarios. This topic teaches students how to systematically identify and document the full spectrum of usage paths.

Elements.Title: What Are Edge Cases?
Elements.BodyText: Edge cases are scenarios that occur at the boundary of normal operating conditions, involving unusual inputs, extreme values, or rare but valid user behaviors. Failing to account for edge cases is a frequent source of system defects and poor user experience.
Elements.Notes: Edge cases differ from exceptions in that they represent valid but infrequent scenarios rather than error conditions. Both must be documented, but they call for different system responses.

Items.Text: Edge cases involve boundary conditions such as maximum field lengths or minimum valid values.
They often involve unusual but permitted combinations of user choices or system states.
Edge cases that are not designed for intentionally are handled inconsistently or incorrectly.
User research and task analysis are primary sources for identifying real-world edge cases.

Elements.Title: Techniques for Enumerating Usage Paths
Elements.BodyText: Systematic enumeration of usage paths ensures that requirements coverage is complete rather than representative. Several structured techniques help analysts move beyond obvious scenarios to discover the full interaction space.
Elements.Notes: Combining multiple enumeration techniques is recommended. Any single technique will miss some scenarios that others surface.

Items.Text: Flow analysis traces every branch in a task model to ensure all paths are represented as use cases.
Boundary value analysis identifies the edges of acceptable input ranges for each system parameter.
Negative testing considers what users might do that the system should reject or handle gracefully.
Scenario-based reviews with diverse stakeholders surface paths that analysts may not anticipate.

Elements.Title: User Diversity and Context Variation
Elements.BodyText: Users differ in experience level, accessibility needs, device capabilities, and operating environments, all of which create distinct interaction paths. Designing for diverse users requires explicitly documenting how these differences affect use case flows.
Elements.Notes: Personas are a useful tool for systematically considering user diversity when reviewing use cases. Assigning each use case review to a specific persona prevents the team from defaulting to the assumed average user.

Items.Text: New and experienced users often follow different paths to accomplish the same goal.
Accessibility requirements such as keyboard navigation or screen reader support create distinct flows.
Device and connectivity constraints may require conditional flows for low-bandwidth or mobile contexts.
Cultural and localization differences can affect input formats, workflow assumptions, and error messages.

Elements.Title: Documenting Frequency and Priority
Elements.BodyText: Not all use cases are equally important or frequent, and documenting their relative frequency and business priority helps teams focus design and development effort appropriately. Priority ratings also guide testing and risk management.
Elements.Notes: Frequency data can be gathered from existing system analytics, user surveys, or expert estimates. Priority is typically assigned by stakeholders based on business value and risk.

Items.Text: High-frequency use cases should receive the most design iteration and usability testing.
Low-frequency but high-consequence use cases such as emergency procedures require equal rigor.
Priority ratings should be agreed upon by stakeholders, not assigned unilaterally by analysts.
Frequency and priority metadata help teams make informed tradeoffs when scope is constrained.

Elements.Title: Reviewing for Completeness
Elements.BodyText: A structured review process is needed to confirm that the complete use case set covers all identified actors, goals, tasks, and interaction contexts without redundancy or gaps. Completeness reviews should involve multiple stakeholders.
Elements.Notes: Coverage matrices that map actors to use cases are an effective tool for spotting gaps. Every actor should have at least one use case, and every stated stakeholder goal should be traceable to at least one scenario.

Items.Text: Actor-to-use-case matrices visualize coverage and reveal actors with missing scenarios.
Goal-to-use-case traceability ensures every stakeholder need is addressed.
Peer reviews by developers and testers often surface overlooked technical edge cases.
Iterative reviews should be scheduled as new requirements are added or existing ones change.

Topics.Title: Documenting and Communicating Requirements
Topics.Summary: Well-written use cases only deliver value if they are organized, communicated, and maintained effectively as shared project artifacts. This topic covers best practices for documentation, traceability, and stakeholder communication.

Elements.Title: Organizing a Use Case Repository
Elements.BodyText: A use case repository organizes all scenarios in a structured, searchable, and version-controlled format that supports ongoing project work. Effective organization ensures that use cases remain a living reference rather than a static document.
Elements.Notes: Repositories can range from simple structured documents to dedicated requirements management tools such as JIRA, Confluence, or specialized platforms like IBM DOORS. The choice should match the team's size and process maturity.

Items.Text: Use cases should be grouped by actor, functional area, or system module for navigability.
A consistent naming and numbering scheme enables reliable cross-referencing and traceability.
Version control ensures that changes to use cases are tracked and previous versions are recoverable.
Access permissions should be configured so stakeholders can review but only authorized team members can edit.

Elements.Title: Traceability Between Requirements and Use Cases
Elements.BodyText: Traceability links use cases to the stakeholder needs, system requirements, design decisions, and test cases they relate to. Maintaining traceability ensures that every requirement is implemented and tested.
Elements.Notes: Bidirectional traceability allows teams to assess the impact of a requirement change by identifying all use cases and downstream artifacts affected. This is especially important for regulated industries.

Items.Text: Each use case should be traceable to at least one source stakeholder need or business goal.
Forward traceability links use cases to design elements and implementation tasks.
Backward traceability links test cases back to the use cases they verify.
Traceability matrices should be updated whenever requirements or use cases change.

Elements.Title: Communicating Use Cases to Stakeholders
Elements.BodyText: Use cases must be presented in a format accessible to the intended audience, which varies from technical developers to non-technical business stakeholders. Tailoring communication style and detail level improves stakeholder engagement and review quality.
Elements.Notes: Visual representations such as use case diagrams, storyboards, or wireframe walkthroughs can make scenarios more accessible to non-technical audiences. Written use cases remain the authoritative specification.

Items.Text: Executive summaries of use case coverage help business stakeholders evaluate scope.
Use case diagrams provide a high-level visual overview of actors and interactions.
Walkthroughs where stakeholders step through scenarios interactively improve review quality.
Technical audiences such as developers and testers should have access to the full detailed specification.

Elements.Title: Maintaining Use Cases Through Change
Elements.BodyText: Requirements evolve throughout a project, and use cases must be updated to reflect approved changes in a timely and controlled manner. A change management process prevents use cases from becoming outdated or contradictory.
Elements.Notes: Change requests should trigger a review of all use cases potentially affected, not just the one explicitly mentioned. Failing to propagate changes consistently is a leading cause of defects late in development.

Items.Text: A formal change request process should govern any modification to approved use cases.
Impact analysis should identify all use cases and dependent artifacts affected by a proposed change.
Updated use cases should be re-reviewed and re-approved by relevant stakeholders.
A changelog within each use case document records who changed what and when.

Elements.Title: Use Cases as Input to Design and Testing
Elements.BodyText: Use case scenarios are a primary input for interface design, providing designers with the task flows and interaction contexts needed to create relevant prototypes and wireframes. They also serve as the basis for acceptance test case development.
Elements.Notes: Designers should be involved in use case reviews to ensure scenarios are feasible and to identify interaction design implications early. Testers should begin drafting acceptance test cases as soon as use cases are approved.

Items.Text: Each main and alternative flow in a use case maps to at least one interface design scenario.
Exception flows identify error states that the interface design must explicitly address.
Acceptance test cases can be derived directly from use case step sequences and postconditions.
Early designer and tester involvement in use case review improves downstream artifact quality.
